newsitem.title: UK: Britain's Rifkind warns EU "flexibility" limited.
newsitem.headline: Britain's Rifkind warns EU "flexibility" limited.

text.p: British Foreign Secretary Malcolm Rifkind warned on Thursday that French and German plans to allow some European Union states to integrate faster than others would have to be approved by all 15 member states.
Paris and Bonn on Tuesday unveiled their long-awaited plan designed to allow EU states to push ahead with joint ventures without being held up by reluctant partners such as Britain.
But Rifkind said on Thursday that any cooperation venture which involved European institutions or funds would require unanimous approval before a small group could go ahead.
"Any group of countries can join together by their own initiative and do certain things jointly.
"If they wish, however, and this is a fundamental British position, ...to have access to European Union institutions, that is only acceptable if 15 states agree," Rifkind told parliament.

"That is not for some theoretical or ideological reason, it is because having access to European institutions means the European Commission will be involved, the European Court will be involved and the budget will be involved."

France and Germany say the issue, known in EU jargon as "flexibility", is one of the most crucial facing the bloc as it rewrites its treaty to prepare for the future and the entry of new members from eastern Europe and the Mediterranean.
"The system we have set up for 15 countries will certainly not work for 25 or 30," said German State Secretary Werner Hoyer on Tuesday, referring to the EU's planned enlargement.

Germany and France want a new clause in the EU treaty -- under review in the so-called inter-governmental conference (IGC) due to end next June -- making it clear some states can move ahead of others in areas of European cooperation.
Rifkind said he was not against cooperation ventures like the Schengen pact on open borders. Britain's worry is over pacts involving EU funds and institutions like the court of justice.
"A lot more work needs to be done...," Rifkind said.

"None of us have any doubts that the European union of the future will be flexible... it is how it will work, what the institutional implications will be and how the interests of minorities as well as majorities can be properly safeguarded."

Rifkind made clear this also did not mean flexible cooperation was impossible. The single European currency will involve small groups moving forward without others. But it was approved by all 15 states before it could proceed.
But Rifkind warned that a rush to accept flexible pacts without considering the consequences was dangerous.
Rifkind's statement is likely to heighten once again the rifts between Britain, which is opposed to deeper political and economic integration, and its EU partners.
